proposals.impact: lift open rate on Money Worship and Money Avoidance sequences toward Vigilance's 66.67% baseline
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has a 66.67% open rate across 12 sends. Money Worship sits at 37.5% (16 sends) and Money Avoidance at 52.63% (19 sends). That gap is meaningful at these sample sizes. The Vigilance sequence is clearly hitting the reader's existing internal state more precisely. The subject lines and opening hooks in Vigilance are almost certainly more specific and less reassuring in tone, which matches what a vigilance-type reader already suspects about themselves. Worship subscribers are leaving 63% of emails unopened, which is the sharpest drop-off in the funnel right now.
proposals.proposal: Pull the subject line and preview text from the first email in the Money Vigilance sequence and apply the same structural logic to the Money Worship sequence's first email. The Vigilance sequence likely earns its open rate by naming something the reader is already quietly thinking — not promising a fix, but reflecting a recognisable moment back at them. The Worship sequence's 37.5% rate suggests its subject line is either too generic or too reassuring for someone who ties their self-worth to their balance sheet. Rewrite the Money Worship email 1 subject line and preview text to mirror that sharper, more honest register. No new content to write. One file, one diff.

---
title: "Why earning more hasn't made me feel any safer"
pubDate: 2026-07-14
description: "The pay rise landed. The promotion came through. The number went up. And somehow the low-grade anxiety about money didn't move."
tags: ["money worship", "self-worth", "behavioural finance"]
---

The pay rise landed. The promotion came through. The number in the account went up.

And the low-grade anxiety about money didn't move.

If you're reading this, you probably already know that feeling. You hit the target you'd set yourself, then immediately reset it upward, and the window of relief lasted about four days.

This isn't a discipline problem. It isn't because you haven't read the right book or built the right spreadsheet.

Joel works with clients who earn well and still feel financially precarious. Not because their numbers are bad, but because their sense of safety has never actually been tied to the numbers — even when they believed it was.

The pattern has a name in behavioural research: money worship. The working assumption is that more money will eventually resolve the discomfort. It rarely does, because the discomfort isn't coming from the balance. It's coming from something the balance was always too blunt an instrument to address.

That doesn't mean the money doesn't matter. It means the work underneath the money matters too.

If the number going up has never quite been enough, that's worth sitting with — not as a flaw, but as honest information about what's actually driving the feeling.

Joel is an MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner working with clients in the UK. If this landed, the [quiz is a reasonable starting point](/quiz).
